request: Show the forces on a crate resting on a ramp.

commands.speak: Let's find every force acting on a crate resting on a ramp.
The ramp rises at thirty degrees.
Here is the crate, sitting still on the slope.
Gravity pulls it straight down, no matter how the ramp tilts.
The ramp pushes back at a right angle to its surface — the normal force.
And friction acts up the slope, holding the crate against sliding.
Because the crate is at rest, these three forces balance exactly.

request: Draw a benzene ring.

commands.speak: This is benzene, the simplest aromatic ring.
Six carbon atoms form a perfect hexagon — every unlabeled corner is a carbon.
The inner lines mark alternating double bonds — in reality the electrons are shared evenly around the whole ring.
That shared electron cloud is what makes benzene unusually stable.

request: Show a protein's secondary structure.

commands.speak: A protein chain folds into a few recurring local shapes — its secondary structure.
Reading from the N terminus, the chain starts as a flexible loop.
Then it coils into an alpha helix, held together by hydrogen bonds along the backbone.
Another short loop turns the chain around.
Here it stretches out into a beta strand, drawn as a flat arrow.
And a final loop carries the chain to the C terminus.

request: Draw the structure of aspirin.
title: Aspirin

commands.speak: This is aspirin — one of the oldest medicines still in daily use. Let's build its structure.
The skeleton first: every unlabeled corner is a carbon atom.
The circle marks the aromatic benzene ring at its core.
Two carbon-oxygen double bonds — one in the acid group, one in the ester.
And here are the oxygens: the acid group that makes it aspirin, and the acetyl group that makes it gentle enough to swallow.
That's acetylsalicylic acid. Click the 3D button on this figure to explore the real three-dimensional structure.

request: Show demand shifting right and animate the new equilibrium.

commands.speak: Let's watch a market adjust when demand shifts.
Quantity sits on the horizontal axis, price on the vertical.
This downward-sloping line is demand: as price falls, buyers want more.
This upward-sloping line is supply: higher prices draw out more sellers.
Where the two lines cross is equilibrium — the price and quantity the market settles on.
Here's a copy of the demand curve — right now it sits exactly on top of the original.
Its equilibrium starts right where today's market already clears.
Now incomes rise — at every price, buyers want more, so the whole curve slides to the right.
Where it crosses supply, both price and quantity have risen — compare the old and new equilibrium.

request: Draw a decision tree comparing surgery with medication, with probabilities and QALYs.

commands.speak: Let's work out which treatment we should expect to give the patient more good years.
The square is the choice we control: surgery or medication.
Take surgery first. The circle means what happens next is chance, not choice.
Nine times in ten it works, and the patient gains nine and a half quality-adjusted life years.
One time in ten there's a complication, and only four.
Medication is a gamble too, just a gentler one.
Seven times in ten the disease is controlled at seven and a half years; otherwise five.
Now fold the tree back: nine point five times nought point nine, plus four times nought point one, is eight point nine five for surgery.
The same sum for medication gives six point seven five.
Surgery wins on expected QALYs — and that number, not the best case, is what we weigh against its cost.

request: Show the QALYs gained from a treatment compared with no treatment.

commands.speak: A QALY is a year of life weighted by how good that year is. Let's see what a treatment buys.
Age runs across, quality of life up: one is perfect health, zero is death.
Without treatment, this patient falls ill at forty-five and declines until seventy.
With treatment the story changes — but look closely at what happens first.
The red sliver is real: the first months of treatment are worse than no treatment at all.
Then the patient recovers to a better level, and lives twelve years longer.
The green area minus the red one is the QALYs gained — the whole benefit in a single number.
Divide the cost of the treatment by that area and you have the cost per QALY.

request: Explain what mitochondria do.

commands.speak: Let's find the part of the cell that turns food into usable energy.
Here's an animal cell, wrapped in a double-layered membrane.
The nucleus holds the instructions — but it doesn't power anything.
This bean-shaped compartment is a mitochondrion, and this is where the energy comes from.
Its inner membrane folds back and forth into ridges called cristae.
Those folds pack a huge working surface into a tiny space — and the energy reactions happen on that surface.
More folds mean more power, which is why a heart muscle cell is crowded with mitochondria.

request: Show why a magnifying glass makes a virtual image.

commands.speak: A magnifying glass makes things look bigger — let's see where that bigger picture actually is.
Here's the lens, seen edge-on, with the optical axis running through its centre.
Each F marks a focal point, twelve centimetres out on either side.
Now put the object just seven centimetres away — closer than the focal point.
One ray leaves the tip parallel to the axis, and the lens bends it through the far focal point.
A second goes straight through the centre, undeflected.
Notice the problem: after the lens the two rays spread apart. They never cross, so there is no picture to catch on a screen.
So we trace them backwards instead, dashed, to where they seem to come from.
There they meet: an upright, magnified, virtual image — behind the glass, on the same side as the object.
That is the whole trick of a magnifying glass: your eye is fooled into seeing this larger version.

request: Show how a catalyst lowers the activation energy.

commands.speak: A catalyst speeds a reaction up without being used up. Let's see how, on an energy diagram.
Energy runs up the side; across the bottom is the progress of the reaction.
We start here, with the reactants.
And we end lower down, with the products — energy is released.
But the molecules cannot slide straight down: first they must climb over this hump.
That climb is the activation energy — the reason a mixture can sit unreacted for years.
A catalyst opens a different route over the barrier, a lower one.
Now far more molecules have enough energy to get across, so the reaction runs much faster.
And look what did not change: the drop from reactants to products is exactly the same.
A catalyst changes the road, never the destination.

request: Draw the DNA double helix and explain base pairing.

commands.speak: DNA stores your genetic instructions in a shape worth drawing carefully.
One strand of sugar and phosphate winds through space like a spiral staircase rail.
A second rail runs alongside it, half a turn out of step.
Between them sit the base pairs: A always with T, C always with G.
Each rung is one letter of the code, and the pairing rule means either rail alone can rebuild the other.
That is why the helix can be unzipped and copied — the shape is the mechanism.

request: Explain what wavelength and amplitude mean.

commands.speak: Two numbers describe almost any wave. Let's read them straight off the picture.
This line is the resting position — where the water, or the air, sits undisturbed.
The wave rises above it and dips below it, over and over.
The high points are crests, the low points troughs.
Amplitude is the height from rest up to a crest — how strong the wave is. Louder sound, taller amplitude.
Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next — the length of one full repeat.
Squeeze the wavelength and the wave repeats more often each second: that is a higher frequency, and a higher pitch.
Amplitude is how big, wavelength is how often — and they are independent of each other.

request: Draw the combustion of methane.

commands.speak: When natural gas burns, atoms are rearranged — never created or destroyed. Let's check that.
We start with one methane molecule and two oxygen molecules.
A spark supplies the heat that gets the reaction going.
Out comes carbon dioxide and two waters.
Now count: one carbon each side, four hydrogens each side, four oxygens each side.
That balance is what makes it an equation rather than a story — and it is why the coefficients cannot be chosen freely.

request: Compare diffusion and active transport across a cell membrane.

commands.speak: Some things drift into a cell for free. Others have to be pushed, and pushing costs energy.
The membrane is two rows of phospholipids: water-loving heads facing out, oily tails meeting in the middle.
This protein is a channel — an open pore through the oily middle.
Oxygen is plentiful outside and scarce inside, so it simply drifts down that difference. No energy needed.
This one is a pump, and it works the other way round.
It drives sodium out even though sodium is already scarcer outside — uphill, against the gradient.
That is why the pump burns ATP: going downhill is free, going uphill is not.
Same membrane, same direction of travel — the difference is whether the gradient helps you or fights you.

request: How are humans, chimps, mice, rats and chickens related?

commands.speak: A family tree of species reads from the tips inwards. Let's read this one.
Five living species sit at the tips — nobody here is descended from anybody else here.
Every fork behind them is a common ancestor that split into two lines.
Human and chimp meet at the shallowest fork, so their shared ancestor is the most recent.
The chicken branches off deepest, further back in time than any of the others.
Read the forks, not the drawing order: closeness on this tree means a more recent ancestor, not looking alike.

request: Show sensitivity and specificity in a 2×2 test-versus-disease table.

commands.speak: Sensitivity and specificity both come from the same 2×2 table — test result against true disease status.
Rows are the test result; columns are whether the patient truly has the disease.
True positive — the test is positive, and the patient really has the disease.
False positive — a positive test, but no disease.
False negative — the test misses a real case.
And true negative, where the test correctly clears a healthy patient.
Sensitivity looks at this whole disease-present column: true positives over true positives plus false negatives.
Specificity looks at the disease-absent column the same way: true negatives over true negatives plus false positives.

request: Draw a timeline of a research project.

commands.speak: Here's how a typical research project unfolds, from kickoff to publication.
The timeline runs from the project's start to where things stand today.
First, the protocol is approved and the team is ready to begin.
Then data collection — usually the longest stretch.
The analysis is where the findings actually take shape.
And finally, the manuscript goes out for submission.
Four milestones, one straight line from question to publication.

request: Draw a production function with diminishing returns.

commands.speak: As you add more labor to a fixed amount of capital, output keeps rising — but each extra worker adds less than the last.
Labor along the bottom, total output up the side.
The production function climbs steeply at first, then flattens out.
That flattening is diminishing returns: the curve is concave, even though output never falls.

request: Draw a three-state Markov model: Well, Sick, Dead.

commands.speak: A Markov model follows people between health states over repeated cycles.
Three states: well, sick, and dead.
Well and sick are both transient — you can stay in either from one cycle to the next.
Ten percent of the time, someone well becomes sick.
And thirty percent of the time, someone sick recovers to well.
Both states can also lead to death, at their own separate rates.
Death is absorbing: once you arrive, no arrow leads back out.
That's the whole cycle: well, sick, and the one state nobody leaves.

request: Show two treatments on a cost-effectiveness plane with a WTP threshold of 30,000 per QALY.

commands.speak: A cost-effectiveness plane compares treatments by both their cost and their effect at once.
Effect runs left to right, cost runs bottom to top, both zeroed on the comparator.
Each quadrant tells a different story: costing more or less, working better or worse.
This dashed line is what we're willing to pay: thirty thousand per QALY gained.
The new drug adds a little effect for a modest cost — well under the threshold.
Surgery adds more effect, but costs far more than the threshold allows.
Same plane, two very different value propositions.

request: Draw the prisoner's dilemma and show the Nash equilibrium.

commands.speak: Two suspects are questioned separately. Let's see why they might both confess, even though staying silent would serve them better.
Each suspect can cooperate with their partner by staying silent, or defect by confessing.
If both stay silent, they each get a light sentence — a payoff of three.
But if one confesses while the other stays silent, the confessor goes free and the other takes the fall.
If both confess, they both do worse than if they had cooperated.
Look at the underlines: confessing is the best response no matter what the other suspect does.
That makes mutual confession the Nash equilibrium — even though silence would have left them both better off.

request: Show how a consumer chooses the bundle that maximizes their utility.

commands.speak: A consumer has a fixed budget and two things to spend it on. Let's find the combination that makes them happiest.
Coffee along the bottom, books up the side.
The budget line marks every combination they can just afford.
This lower curve is attainable, but there's room to do better without spending more.
This curve just touches the budget line — every point on it gives the same satisfaction.
This higher curve would feel even better, but it's out of reach at this budget.
The optimum sits exactly where the budget line just touches the highest curve they can reach.
Move spending either direction from that point, and total satisfaction only falls.

request: Draw a production possibilities frontier with an unattainable combination of goods.

spec.title: Guns, butter, and why the frontier bows

commands.speak: Guns along the bottom, butter up the side. An economy has only so many workers and machines — so which mixes of the two can it actually make?
Start with the obvious answer: all butter at one end, all guns at the other, and a steady swap in between. That gives a straight line — a constant trade-off.
But that line assumes every worker is equally good at both jobs. Why should the real frontier bow outward instead?
Because resources are not interchangeable. The land and the workers best suited to butter are not the ones best suited to guns.
Move the gun-suited workers over first and you give up hardly any butter — so a mixed economy sits out here, beyond the straight line.
Everything under this production possibilities frontier is attainable. On the curve itself, every resource is already busy — that is an efficient combination.
This mix sits outside. No rearrangement of today's resources reaches it — only more resources, or better technology, moves the whole frontier out.
Read the curve left to right: flat at first, steep at the end. Each extra gun costs more butter than the last — increasing opportunity cost, and the reason the frontier bows.

request: Show the deadweight loss created by a monopoly.

commands.speak: A monopolist restricts output to raise its price — and that costs society more than it gains the firm. Let's see the loss.
Quantity runs along the bottom, price and cost up the side.
This rising curve is marginal cost — what one more unit costs to produce.
This is average total cost, fixed costs and all, spread over output.
Demand shows what price the market will bear at each quantity.
Marginal revenue falls twice as fast — selling one more unit means a lower price on every unit sold.
The monopolist produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, then charges whatever price demand allows at that quantity.
A competitive market would have kept producing further, out to where price equals marginal cost.
This triangle is the deadweight loss: trades that would have benefited both buyer and seller, but never happen.

request: Show aggregate demand shifting right and animate the new equilibrium.

commands.speak: Let's watch the economy adjust when aggregate demand rises.
Real GDP along the bottom, the price level up the side.
This downward-sloping line is aggregate demand.
This upward-sloping line is aggregate supply.
Where they cross is the economy's equilibrium — its price level and output today.
Here's a copy of aggregate demand — right now it sits exactly on top of the original.
Its equilibrium starts right on top of today's.
Now suppose spending rises across the economy — the whole AD curve slides to the right.
Compare old and new: both output and the price level have risen — the signature of a demand-driven expansion.

request: Compare survival on treatment versus control.

commands.speak: Let's compare how long patients survive on treatment versus control.
Time along the bottom, the proportion still surviving up the side.
This staircase is the treatment arm — each drop marks patients who didn't make it to the next checkpoint.
This lower curve is the control arm — it falls faster and further.
This tick mark is a censored patient — one who left the study early, without an event.
Follow the dashed line at fifty percent survival: the control arm crosses it, giving its median survival time.
Treatment's curve stays clearly above control's the whole way through.
The gap between the two curves is the treatment effect.

request: Draw a meta-analysis forest plot pooling four studies.

spec.title: Pooling four trials in a forest plot

commands.speak: Four trials tested the same treatment. Let's combine their evidence into one meta-analysis.
Risk ratio sits on a log scale, so equal fold-changes are equally spaced — one means no effect.
This dashed line marks a risk ratio of one: no difference between treatment and control.
Anderson's trial found a risk ratio below one, but its interval crosses the line — not significant on its own.
Bianchi's larger trial — the bigger square — found a clearer reduction in risk.
Carter's trial leans the same direction but is smaller and less precise.
Diallo's trial shows the strongest effect.
Pooling all four — weighting the larger trials more — gives this diamond, spanning the pooled confidence interval.
The whole diamond sits left of the null line: together, the evidence supports a real reduction in risk.
Every trial, and the pooled estimate, in one figure.

request: Show how a confounder biases the effect of coffee on heart disease.

params.edges: Coffee -> Heart disease; Stress -> Coffee; Stress -> Heart disease
params.title: Confounding by stress

commands.speak: Coffee drinkers often have worse heart-disease outcomes — but is coffee really the cause?
Here's our exposure: coffee consumption.
And our outcome: heart disease.
The naive story is a direct arrow from coffee straight to heart disease.
But stress causes people to drink more coffee — and stress itself raises heart-disease risk.
Stress points to BOTH coffee and heart disease — that's a classic confounder.
These two tinted arrows are the backdoor path: stress creates an association between coffee and heart disease even if coffee does nothing at all.
Without adjusting for stress, we'd wrongly blame the coffee.

request: Draw an SEIR model of an epidemic with waning immunity.

commands.speak: An SEIR model splits an epidemic into four stages people move through.
Everyone starts susceptible — able to catch the disease.
Exposure moves people into the E box — infected, but not yet infectious themselves.
After an incubation period, they become infectious and can spread the disease onward.
Eventually they recover.
This curved arrow is waning immunity — some recovered people slowly become susceptible again.
The rate of that exposed-to-infectious step is what makes an epidemic explosive or slow.

request: Explain a p-value cutoff of 0.05, two-sided.

commands.speak: A p-value cutoff of 0.05, two-sided, means we split five percent of the area between both tails of the curve.
This is the normal distribution of a test statistic under the null hypothesis — no real effect.
Its center, the mean, is where we'd expect the statistic to land if nothing were going on.
Marked here in standard deviations from that center.
We shade the most extreme five percent — two and a half percent in each tail, beyond about 1.96 standard deviations.
A result landing in either shaded region is considered too unlikely to happen by chance alone.
Land in the white middle, and we fail to reject the null. Land in the shade, and we call it significant.
Same logic underlies almost every significance test in this field.

request: Draw a Venn diagram of two sets and shade their intersection.

commands.speak: Let's look at two overlapping sets.
Everything inside this box is our universe — everything we're considering.
This circle is set A.
And this one is set B.
Where they overlap is A intersect B — elements that belong to both sets.

request: Show the unit circle at a 30 degree angle, and animate it sweeping forward to 330 degrees.

commands.speak: Let's explore the unit circle.
Here's a circle of radius one, centered at the origin.
This radius reaches out to a point on the circle, at an angle of 30 degrees.
That's the angle theta, measured from the positive x-axis.
The horizontal distance to the point is its cosine.
And the vertical distance is its sine.
Together they give the point's exact coordinates.
Watch as the angle sweeps forward, almost all the way around the circle, to 330 degrees.

request: Show the solution to x is greater than 1 on a number line.

commands.speak: Let's solve x is greater than 1 on a number line.
Here's our number line, from zero to five.
At 1, we draw an open circle, since x can't equal 1 itself — just be greater than it.
Everything to the right is shaded: every value greater than 1 solves the inequality.

request: Prove Thales' theorem: an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.

commands.speak: Let's prove Thales' theorem.
Take any circle, and draw a diameter across it.
This is the diameter, from A to B.
Label its two ends A and B.
Now pick any point C on the circle, and connect it to both ends of the diameter.
No matter where C sits on the circle, the angle at C is always a right angle — that's Thales' theorem.

request: Make a truth table for (A AND B) OR NOT A.

spec.title: Truth table: (A AND B) OR NOT A

commands.speak: Let's build a truth table for (A and B) or not A.
Two variables, A and B — and here's our expression as the header.
Every combination of true and false for A and B, one row each.
When A and B are both false, A and B is false — but not A is true, so the whole expression is true.
Same story here.
But when A is true and B is false, both halves fail, and the expression is false.
And when both are true, A and B alone makes it true.

request: Draw a modus ponens argument map: if it rains the ground gets wet, and it is raining, so the ground is wet.

premises.text: If it rains, the ground gets wet.

commands.speak: Let's map out a classic argument: modus ponens.
Our first premise: if it rains, the ground gets wet.
Our second premise: it is raining.
So we conclude: the ground is wet.
Both premises support the conclusion — together, they guarantee it.

request: Show the quadratic formula.

commands.speak: Let's derive the quadratic formula, step by step.
We start with the general form of a quadratic equation.
Here it is: a x squared, plus b x, plus c, equals zero.
Completing the square gets us here.
And solving for x gives us the quadratic formula.

request: Explain E = mc^2.

steps.note: Energy equals mass times the speed of light, squared.
c² alone is a huge number — about 90 quadrillion (m/s)².

commands.speak: Let's unpack Einstein's most famous equation.
Mass-energy equivalence.
E is energy, m is mass, and c is the speed of light — about three hundred million meters per second.
Squaring c makes this multiplier enormous, so even a tiny mass converts into a huge amount of energy.

request: Show Euler's identity.

steps.note: Euler's formula — links the exponential to rotation.
Set x = π: cos π = -1, sin π = 0.

commands.speak: This is often called the most beautiful equation in mathematics.
Euler's identity.
Euler's formula: e to the i x equals cosine x plus i sine x — it links exponentials to rotation around a circle.
Set x to pi: cosine of pi is minus one, and sine of pi is zero.
That leaves e to the i pi, plus one, equals zero — five fundamental constants, e, i, pi, one and zero, meeting in a single equation.

request: Explain Bayes' theorem.

steps.note: The probability of A, given that B happened.
D = has the disease, T = tests positive.

commands.speak: Bayes' theorem updates a belief once new evidence comes in.
Bayes' theorem.
The probability of A given B equals the probability of B given A, times the probability of A, divided by the probability of B.

In a diagnostic test: the chance you actually have the disease given a positive result equals how likely a positive test is when you're sick, times how common the disease is, divided by how likely a positive result is overall — posterior equals likelihood times prior, divided by evidence.

request: Show the saddle surface z = x squared minus y squared, and walk around it in 3D.

spec.title: The saddle surface z = x² − y²

commands.speak: A wireframe lets us see a 3D surface without it hiding what's behind it.
Here are the x, y and z axes.
This is the saddle surface z equals x squared minus y squared — it curves up along one direction and down along the other.
From this side, the surface rises on both arms toward us.
Now watch the ridge become a valley as we come around to the other side.

request: Draw a 3D helix.

commands.speak: A helix is a curve that spirals steadily upward, like a spring or a strand of DNA's backbone.
Here are the x, y and z axes.
As the angle t sweeps around and around, x is cosine t, y is sine t, and z climbs steadily as t over six.
Let's orbit around it to see the spiral from every side.

request: Draw a series circuit with a battery, a bulb and a switch.

commands.speak: Let's build a simple series circuit and watch the current flow around it.
Here's the loop of wire the current will travel around.
The battery always sits in the bottom wire — it's what drives the current.
In series, the lamp is spliced right into the loop.
And so is the switch — open it, and the whole loop breaks.
Conventional current flows clockwise, out of the battery's positive terminal, through every component in turn, and back in the negative side.

request: Show projectile motion at 45 degrees.

commands.speak: Let's launch a projectile and trace out its path.
Here's the ground it launches from and lands on.
Ignoring air resistance, gravity bends its path into a perfect parabola.
It leaves the ground at this velocity, angled up and to the right.
At the very top, all the vertical motion is gone — the velocity is purely horizontal.
By the time it lands, it's moving just as fast as it launched, mirrored below the horizontal.
Now watch what happens as we steepen the launch angle: the same speed sends it higher, but not as far.

request: Draw the MAPK-style pathway EGFR to RAS to ERK, with p53 inhibiting the cell cycle.

params.edges: EGFR -> RAS; RAS -> ERK; p53 -| cell cycle
params.title: A simplified MAPK cascade

commands.speak: Cells relay outside signals inward through chains of proteins that switch each other on or off.
It starts at the cell surface, with a receptor like EGFR.
EGFR activates RAS, the next protein in the chain.
RAS in turn activates ERK, which goes on to switch on genes for cell division.
Meanwhile p53, the cell's damage sensor, can inhibit the cell cycle directly — the bar-headed arrow means 'blocks', not 'activates'.
Together, this is a simplified MAPK cascade — one of the most common signaling motifs in biology.

request: Cross two heterozygous parents in a Punnett square.

commands.speak: Let's cross two heterozygous parents and predict their offspring.
A Punnett square lays out every possible combination of the parents' alleles.
Each parent is heterozygous, Aa, so each contributes either an A gamete or an a gamete.
Combining them gives four possible offspring genotypes: AA, Aa, Aa, and aa.
Only the aa offspring shows the recessive trait — every other combination carries at least one dominant allele.
That's the classic 3 to 1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes.

request: Draw a food web with grass, rabbits, mice, foxes and hawks.

commands.speak: Energy flows up through an ecosystem in a food web, from producers to predators.
We'll lay it out in bands: producers at the bottom, rising through primary and secondary consumers to apex predators at the top.
Grass is a producer — it makes its own energy from sunlight.
Rabbits and mice are primary consumers: they eat the grass.
A fox is a secondary consumer, eating the rabbits and mice.
And a hawk sits at the top as an apex predator.
Each arrow points from prey to predator — from what's eaten, up to what eats it.

request: Draw the Lewis structure of water.

commands.speak: Water's Lewis structure shows exactly how its electrons are shared and held.
Oxygen sits at the center, with six valence electrons of its own.
It forms one single bond with each hydrogen, sharing one electron pair per bond.
That leaves oxygen with two lone pairs of its own — electrons that aren't shared, and the reason water's shape is bent rather than straight.

request: Show a titration setup with a pink indicator.

commands.speak: Titration measures exactly how much of one solution it takes to react with another.
A retort stand holds everything steady.
The burette, clamped above, delivers titrant one measured drop at a time.
Below it sits the flask, holding the solution being tested.
A few drops of indicator turn the solution pink right at the endpoint — the signal to stop adding titrant.

request: Show the Scholar's Mate.
title: Scholar's Mate

commands.speak: Here's the opening position — a fresh game of chess.
1. e4 — White opens with the king's pawn.
e5 — Black mirrors it.
Bc4 — the bishop takes aim at f7, Black's weakest square.
Nc6 — Black develops a knight and defends e5.
Qh5 — the queen joins the attack, eyeing f7.
Nf6, attacking the queen — but missing the real threat.
Qxf7 checkmate! The queen captures on f7, and there's no escape.
This is Scholar's mate — the fastest common checkmate in chess.

request: Where are the Nordic countries?
title: The Nordic countries

commands.speak: Let's find the Nordic countries — Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland and Iceland.
Here they are, cropped in from the world map so they fill the frame.
Norway traces the western coast, its fjord-cut edge shading in.
Their capitals: Oslo, Stockholm, Copenhagen, Helsinki and Reykjavik.
Five countries, one shared region at the top of Europe.

request: Explain opportunity cost with a dialogue #qa

commands.speak: Every economy has to choose how to split its hours between two things — let's see what that choice really costs.
This bowed curve is the production possibilities frontier: everything on it uses every hour of labor there is.
Everything underneath is attainable; nothing above it is, not with the time we have.
Say we start here, spending most of our hours gathering coconuts.
So moving along the curve is free — we're not really giving anything up either way?
Watch what happens sliding toward more fishing instead: the coconut harvest has to fall — and that drop, the slope of the curve right here, is the opportunity cost of the extra fish.
Oh — so it's not that moving along the curve is free, it's that every extra fish comes straight out of the coconut pile?
Exactly — the frontier's slope at any point is the opportunity cost of producing more of the other good.

request: Does raising the minimum wage help workers? #debate

spec.title: Does a higher minimum wage help workers?

commands.speak: A minimum wage sounds simple: pay workers more. Let's actually test that.
Employers demand less labor as it gets more expensive — this downward curve.
Workers supply more labor at a higher wage — this upward one.
Left alone, the market settles right here — this wage, this many jobs.
Set a wage floor above that. First claim: a free raise for every worker, nobody worse off.
Second claim: it prices the least-skilled workers out of a job entirely.
Here's what the picture actually shows: at that wage, more people want jobs than employers want to fill.
So the first claim doesn't survive the picture — those priced-out workers are the real cost of the floor.

request: Explain how an epidemic spreads #fun

commands.speak: Let's trace how an epidemic spreads — and, just for fun, let's say this one makes zombies.
At rate beta, susceptible people get infected and cross over.
Now they're infectious themselves, able to pass it on to anyone nearby.
At rate gamma, infectious people recover — or are otherwise removed from the chain.
And here's where they land: no longer susceptible, no longer infectious.
The two rates together set the reproduction number. With an R0 of 2, every zombie — every infectious case — bites, or infects, two more before it's stopped.

request: Tell the story of the Phillips curve #story #human #male

commands.speak: Hmm — an engineer, of all people, gave economics one of its most famous curves.
At the London School of Economics, A. W. Phillips combed through British wage records — decade by decade, back to 1861.
He plotted how fast wages rose against how many people were out of work, stretch of years by stretch of years.
By 1957 — almost a century later — he had the whole picture laid out on the page.
Through those scattered years ran a single downward slope: low unemployment, fast-rising wages — high unemployment, wages barely moved.
Phillips published it in 1958. It held for over a decade — until the 1970s, when inflation and unemployment rose together, and the simple trade-off broke.

request: Show what statins change for 100 people like me.

commands.speak: Twenty percent fewer heart attacks — sounds impressive. Let's see what it really means for one hundred people.
Here are one hundred people. For ninety of them, the statin changes nothing — no heart attack either way.
Eight would have a heart attack whether or not they take the pill.
And these two are the entire benefit: two people in a hundred avoid a heart attack because of the statin.
Two in one hundred — that is what twenty percent fewer looks like in absolute terms.
Same drug, same data — but the icon array is the honest picture.

request: Walk me through a normal ECG.

commands.speak: An E C G is drawn on graph paper — every small square is a fifth of a second.
Here is one normal heartbeat after another, about seventy-five per minute.
The little P wave comes first: the atria contracting.
Then the tall spike — the QRS complex — as the ventricles fire.
And the T wave: the ventricles resetting for the next beat.
P, QRS, T — repeated steadily. That is sinus rhythm.

request: Explain how blood flows through the heart and lungs.

commands.speak: Two destinations: the body below, the lungs above.
Between them sits the heart — four chambers, two on each side of a solid wall.
The right side handles blue, oxygen-poor blood.
The left side handles red, oxygen-rich blood.
Used blood returns from the body into the right atrium.
It drops into the right ventricle.
From there it is pumped up to the lungs to collect oxygen.
Fresh red blood flows back into the left atrium.
It fills the powerful left ventricle.
And it is driven out through the aorta to the whole body.
Two loops through one pump — that is the double circulation.

request: Draw a neuron and show how the signal travels.

commands.speak: A neuron listens with its dendrites — branching antennas for incoming signals.
The signals meet in the cell body, where the neuron decides whether to fire.
When it fires, the impulse races down a single long cable: the axon.
Fatty myelin sheaths insulate the cable in segments.
The signal leaps from gap to gap — the nodes of Ranvier — which makes it fast.
It travels one way only: from the cell body toward the terminals.
At the axon terminals the message is handed on to the next cell.

request: Why can screening look better than it is? Show lead-time bias.

commands.speak: Screening can double measured survival without giving anyone a single extra day — this timeline shows the trick.
Follow the same patient twice: first, life without screening.
The disease begins here, silently.
Soon a test could find it — but nobody is looking.
It is diagnosed only when symptoms appear.
From diagnosis to death, this patient survives three years.
Now the same patient, the same disease — with screening.
A screening test catches it two years earlier.
But look at the dashed lines: symptoms and death arrive at exactly the same moments as before.
Measured survival jumps from three years to five — yet nobody lived a single day longer.
The difference is only a head start on the stopwatch: the lead time.
Lead-time bias — why survival statistics can flatter screening.

request: Bacon raises cancer risk by 18 percent — should I panic?

commands.speak: "Daily bacon raises bowel-cancer risk by eighteen percent!" Scary headline. Let's see what it actually means for one hundred people.
Ninety-three of them will never get bowel cancer — bacon or no bacon.
Six would get it anyway, even if they never touched bacon in their lives.
And the whole eighteen percent? It is this one extra person.
Eighteen percent of a small risk is a very small risk: one extra case in a hundred daily bacon eaters.
Relative risk writes the headlines. Absolute risk — one in a hundred — is what should make the decision.

request: What does atrial fibrillation actually look like?

commands.speak: Put two fingers on your wrist. Would you notice if your heart had lost its conductor? Here is what that looks like on paper.
This is atrial fibrillation. Watch the spikes: they land at random — no two gaps alike.
And something is missing. There is no small P wave before each spike, because the atria are not beating at all — they are quivering, hundreds of times a minute.
Doctors call this pulse irregularly irregular: chaos with no pattern to find.
The surprise: many people feel nothing at all. But blood pooling in the quivering atria can clot — which is why this quiet rhythm is a leading cause of stroke.

request: Show me third-degree heart block — and why it doesn't just stop the heart.

commands.speak: Here is a reassuring secret: your heart carries spare pacemakers. This is the rhythm that proves it.
In third-degree block, the electrical wiring between the atria and the ventricles is completely cut.
Count the small P waves: the atria march on at ninety a minute. Now count the tall spikes: only forty. Two rhythms in one heart, each ignoring the other.
Those slow spikes come from a backup pacemaker deep in the ventricles — it wakes up whenever no signal arrives from above.
Forty beats a minute is enough to stay alive — and exactly the finding that earns you an artificial pacemaker.

request: Is a hole in the heart always a disaster?

commands.speak: A baby is born with a hole in the heart. It sounds terrifying — but here is the twist: before birth, every one of us had one, on purpose.
The right side collects used, oxygen-poor blood.
The left side pumps fresh red blood out to the body. The wall between them keeps the two strictly apart.
In the womb the lungs are folded away and useless, so a built-in door between the atria lets blood skip them. At the first breath, it slams shut.
A septal defect is when a hole in the wall stays open — here, between the ventricles.
The strong left side squirts blood back into the right, sending it round the lung loop again and again. That wasted round trip is why a large hole makes a child breathless and tired.
The reassuring part: small holes often close on their own — and the rest can be patched.

request: How fast is a thought? Show me the neuron's wiring.

commands.speak: Stub your toe and you feel it almost at once — yet the message crosses more than a metre of living cable. How? Meet the neuron.
This single cell can stretch from your spinal cord all the way to your toe. One cell, over a metre long.
The speed trick is this fatty insulation — myelin — wrapped around the cable in segments.
The impulse doesn't glide along. It jumps, gap to gap, node to node.
Jumping, it reaches up to a hundred and twenty metres per second — over four hundred kilometres per hour. Without myelin, it would crawl at walking pace.
At the end of the line the signal must cross to the next cell.
And here electricity becomes chemistry: vesicles spill neurotransmitter across the gap, and the message travels on.
That is why the pain arrives before you have even looked down.

request: When does a twice-a-day pill actually reach its working level?

commands.speak: You start a new pill, twice a day. When is the drug actually up and running? The answer is stranger than you'd guess.
The goal is this band — enough to work, not enough to harm: the therapeutic window.
Each arrow is one dose, every twelve hours.
Watch the level climb: every new dose lands on what is left of the old ones, so the sawtooth stacks higher — but by less each time.
Until it levels off here, where each dose exactly replaces what is eliminated: steady state.
Now the surprise: how long that takes depends only on the half-life — about five of them. A bigger dose buys a higher plateau, never a faster one.
Only a loading dose cheats the clock — by jumping instead of climbing.

request: Show me the pressure-volume loop — and what heart failure does to it.

commands.speak: Every heartbeat draws the same secret picture: volume across, pressure up. Cardiologists read whole diseases off this one loop.
One: the ventricle fills quietly, at almost no pressure.
Two: both valves slam shut, and pressure explodes with the volume frozen.
Three: the aortic valve opens, and blood is ejected.
Four: the valves close, pressure collapses, and the cycle restarts. Around this loop, once per beat, a hundred thousand times a day.
The loop's width is the stroke volume — what one beat actually delivers.
And here is the quiet marvel: the loop's area is the work of one beat — about one joule. Over a day, that is enough energy to lift a car ten metres.
This dashed line is the ventricle's strength ceiling: its contractility.
Watch heart failure happen: the ceiling tilts down, and the loop narrows — every beat delivers less.
One loop, one joule — and a diagnosis at a glance.

request: How much urine do your kidneys actually make? Follow one drop through the nephron.

commands.speak: Here is a number to sit with: your kidneys filter one hundred and eighty litres a day — your entire blood plasma, sixty times over. This is where it pours in.
Blood arrives under pressure, is sieved through this capillary tuft, and leaves — while the filtrate drips into the tubule.
And immediately, the un-making begins. The proximal tubule grabs most of it straight back.
All of the glucose. Most of the sodium. Most of the water.
Then the hairpin: the loop of Henle dives deep into the salty medulla and climbs back out.
Going down, water is drawn out; climbing up, salt is pumped out. That countercurrent trick is what lets you concentrate urine.
The distal tubule fine-tunes the last of the sodium under hormonal control.
And the collecting duct makes the final decision — how much water to keep — on orders from a hormone that answers to your thirst.
Of one hundred and eighty litres filtered, less than two actually leave. You brew a bathtub every day — and quietly un-brew ninety-nine percent of it.

request: How do economists check whether a policy actually worked?

commands.speak: Every month a study claims some policy worked. Before believing one, economists look at a picture like this — and the part that matters is not where you'd think.
A policy switches on here.
Each dot is the estimated difference between affected and unaffected groups in one period — whiskers for the uncertainty. Before the policy, the dots hug zero.
After it, they jump — and stay up.
Here is the quiet surprise: the left half is the evidence. Flat pre-treatment dots say the groups were on the same path — so the jump can be pinned on the policy.
No flat left half, no causal claim. That is why referees look left before they look right.

request: How do you measure the effect of something against what never happened?

commands.speak: The effect of a policy is the gap between what happened and what would have happened without it. Half of that pair is unobservable — yet economists measure it anyway.
Start with a group the policy never touched.
The treated group runs parallel to it — until the policy hits, and the two paths part ways.
Now the trick: borrow the control group's path to sketch the treated group's missing future — the dashed road not taken.
The gap between the dashed line and reality is the effect. The untouched group stands in for the world that never happened.
Difference-in-differences: subtract the change you'd have seen anyway from the change you saw.

request: Why do arbitrary cutoffs make economists happy?

commands.speak: A scholarship at exactly 85 points. Medicine at exactly age 65. Arbitrary lines — and secretly, gifts to science.
People just below the cutoff miss the treatment.
People just above it get it. But someone at 84.9 and someone at 85.1 are, for all practical purposes, the same person.
So near the line, the cutoff has quietly run a randomized experiment — and any jump between the two fitted curves belongs to the treatment.
This gap is the effect — no laboratory required.
Regression discontinuity: causal evidence found lying around in bureaucratic rules.

request: Does more schooling really mean higher pay? Show me the data.

commands.speak: Does school pay? A dataset with a hundred thousand people should answer that — but plotted raw, it's an unreadable cloud.
So economists bin: sort everyone by schooling, cut them into twenty equal groups, and plot each group's average. Twenty dots — and suddenly there's a shape.
The fitted line makes it precise: each extra year of schooling lines up with roughly the same percentage bump in earnings.
The surprise is how much the averaging reveals: patterns invisible in a hundred thousand points appear in twenty.
The binned scatter — the workhorse chart of modern applied economics.

request: How can one number describe a whole country's inequality?

commands.speak: Line up a country's people from poorest to richest and ask, as you walk the line: what share of all income have we passed so far?
If everyone earned the same, the answer would climb along this diagonal — twenty percent of the people, twenty percent of the income.
A real country sags below it: in Norway, the poorer half holds well under half the income.
And the deeper the sag, the more unequal the country — Brazil's curve hangs far lower.
The shaded area between diagonal and curve, as a share of the whole triangle, is the Gini coefficient — a nation's entire income distribution folded into one number between zero and one.
Zero would be perfect equality; one, a single person with everything. Most countries live between 0.25 and 0.55.

request: Show what government spending does to interest rates in the IS-LM model.

commands.speak: When a government spends big, does the economy grow, or do interest rates just rise? This diagram answers: both — and says how much of each.
The IS curve collects every combination of output and interest rate where the goods market balances — lower rates, more investment, more output.
The LM curve does the same for money: more output means more demand for money, pushing rates up.
Where they cross, both markets clear at once.
Now the government spends: the IS curve slides right.
Output rises — but climbing along the LM curve, so interest rates rise too, crowding out some private investment on the way.
A curiosity: the most famous Keynesian diagram was never drawn by Keynes — John Hicks sketched it in 1937 to summarize him, and the summary conquered the textbooks.

request: If a country saves more, will it grow faster forever?

commands.speak: Save more, invest more, grow richer forever — it sounds obvious. The Solow model says: only half right, and the half that fails is the interesting one.
Output per worker rises with capital per worker — but flattens, because each extra machine helps less than the last.
A fixed slice of output is saved and invested — the same curve, scaled down.
Meanwhile depreciation and population growth eat capital at a steady rate — a straight line that never flattens.
Where saving just covers the erosion, capital stops growing: the steady state. Beyond it, the straight line outruns the flattening curve — always.
What's left between output and saving is consumption — what the machines are ultimately for.
So saving more buys a richer steady state, not faster growth forever. In the long run, only new ideas — better technology — keep growth alive.

request: Why do threats so often fail? Solve the entry game.

commands.speak: A monopolist growls: enter my market and I'll start a price war. Scary — until you draw the game and read it backwards.
The entrant can stay out: nothing gained, and the incumbent keeps its comfortable two.
Or enter — handing the next move to the incumbent.
Fight, and the price war costs BOTH of them — minus one each.
Accommodate, and they share the market at one apiece.
Now read backwards from the end: if entry ever happens, the incumbent prefers one to minus one — it accommodates. Knowing that, the entrant walks in. The war never comes.
The threat failed because carrying it out would hurt the threatener — backward induction calls that bluff. Credible deterrence needs commitment, not growling.

request: Is the new drug worth its price? Show the acceptability curve.

commands.speak: Is the new drug worth it? Committees want a yes or a no — this curve insists the honest answer is a probability that depends on the price of health.
Every input — effect, cost, side effects — is uncertain, so the analysis is run thousands of times with the dice rolled each time.
The curve reads: at each willingness to pay per healthy year, in what share of those runs does the new drug win?
Standard care holds the mirror image.
At thirty thousand per healthy year — a common benchmark — the new drug wins in well under half the runs.
Only near fifty thousand does it become the better bet more often than not.
So the same drug is a poor buy in one country and a fair one in another — the evidence didn't change, the price of health did.

request: Which uncertain number should we worry about most? Draw a tornado diagram.

commands.speak: A cost-effectiveness result rests on a dozen uncertain numbers. Before trusting it — or funding another study — ask which of them can actually overturn it.
Take each parameter in turn, push it from its lowest plausible value to its highest, and record how far the result swings. The effect estimate swings it enormously — both ways across the base case.
The drug's price matters too.

The near-universal surprise: one or two bars dominate everything. Most of the uncertainty budget lives at the top of the funnel.
So read tornados before commissioning research: the top bar tells you which study is worth paying for.

Out of a thousand people like you, the disease is rare: ten have it, nine hundred ninety do not.
Follow the ten who are sick: the test catches nine of them and misses one.
Nine true positives.
But now follow the nine hundred ninety who are healthy: nine percent of them get a false alarm.
That is eighty-nine false positives — ten times as many as the real ones.
So of the ninety-eight people who test positive, only nine are sick. Your chance is about nine percent — not ninety.
The test is fine. The base rate is the story: when a condition is rare, most alarms are false.

request: Why are averages always bell-shaped, even when the data isn't?

commands.speak: Here is the strangest reliable fact in statistics — the reason polls, lab results and quality control work at all.
Take a lopsided population: incomes, hospital costs, waiting times — a long tail to the right, nothing like a bell.
Now repeatedly draw small samples and plot only their AVERAGES. Already at four per sample, the lopsidedness is almost gone.
Grow the samples and watch: the distribution of averages tightens around the true mean — a clean bell, born from a skewed world.
That is the central limit theorem: averages of almost anything are normal. The bell curve isn't in the data — it's in the averaging.

request: What does 95 percent confidence actually mean?

commands.speak: Somewhere out there is the true value — fixed, unknown, and not going anywhere. Every study is an attempt to trap it.
Each study catches a different sample, so each interval lands somewhere new — this is the dance.
Run twenty studies and look at the pattern: most intervals straddle the dashed line.
Nineteen of twenty caught the truth. One — drawn in red — missed completely, through no fault of its authors.
So ninety-five percent describes the METHOD, not your interval: it's the long-run catch rate of the trap. Any single interval, including the one in the study you just read, may be the red one.

commands.speak: Charles Darwin had the most dangerous idea in biology - and then kept it in a drawer. Let's count the years.
The voyage of the Beagle, 1831: five years of finches, fossils and growing doubts.
By 1837 he sketches a branching tree in a private notebook and writes two words above it: I think.
Then - almost nothing, for two decades. He knew what the idea would unleash. What finally moved him was a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace, who had reached the same conclusion on his own.
On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859 - twenty-two years after those two words in the notebook.
The remarkable part is the gap: the most famous book in biology waited twenty years, and might have waited longer if a rival hadn't forced the drawer open.
Great ideas are not always rushed to print.

request: Explain comparative advantage, with a portrait of David Ricardo.

commands.speak: In 1817, a retired London stockbroker posed a puzzle that still decides where your shirt and your wine come from: should a country that is better at EVERYTHING still trade?
The puzzler: David Ricardo — out of the market at forty-two with a fortune, about to invent modern trade theory.
He answered with two countries and two goods.
Here are his own numbers: the hours of labour each country needs per unit.
Portugal needs eighty hours for wine, ninety for cloth.
England needs more for BOTH: one hundred twenty and one hundred. Portugal is simply better at everything — so common sense says England has nothing to offer.
But look at the RATIOS, not the levels. In wine, Portugal needs a third fewer hours than England — a big edge.
In cloth, the edge is tiny — ninety against one hundred.
So let each country do what it is RELATIVELY best at: Portugal makes the wine, England the cloth — and after trading, BOTH end up with more of both goods than they could make alone.
That is comparative advantage: trade follows relative, not absolute, ability. Even a country worse at everything is still relatively best at something - which is why everyone has something to sell.

Adam Smith, about to publish The Wealth of Nations — the book that begins, of all places, with pins.
Here is what he saw: two ways of running the same ten-man workshop.
A worker doing every step himself — drawing the wire, cutting, sharpening, fitting the head — makes at best twenty pins a day. Ten of them: two hundred.
Smith's factory split the work into eighteen small operations, one or two per man. The same ten workers now made forty-eight THOUSAND pins a day.
Two hundred against forty-eight thousand — a two-hundred-forty-fold gain from nothing but organizing the work differently.
That is the division of labour, the very first idea in the book. Pause and click Smith's portrait — its card opens The Wealth of Nations itself.

request: Why are most published research findings false? Show the base-rate arithmetic, and put the paper itself on the slide: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124
title: Most findings are false

spec.title: Why most published findings are false

elements.of: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False

commands.speak: Take a thousand hypotheses a field might test in a year.
Each one is either really true or really false — and the study either reaches significance or it does not.
Suppose a hundred of the thousand are genuinely true. That is a generous field.
A study with eighty per cent power finds eighty of those hundred, and misses twenty.
Of the nine hundred false hypotheses, a five per cent significance threshold still hands back forty-five significant results.
So a hundred and twenty-five papers report a significant finding — and forty-five of them, more than one in three, are false.
John Ioannidis made exactly this arithmetic famous in 2005; his paper is here — click it to read.
Nothing was fabricated and no rule was broken. The false-discovery rate falls straight out of the base rate, the power, and the threshold.

elements.quote: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely

commands.speak: Four words of one sentence.
A recurrent network had to walk them in order: every word waited for the one before it, so a hundred-word sentence meant a hundred steps that could not be shared out.
Attention throws the queue away — every word looks straight at every other, so "tired" reaches "animal" in one hop instead of two.
The 2017 paper that made this the default architecture said it in a single line of its abstract.
Dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.

And the words that mattered were "dispensing with". Attention was already in use alongside recurrence; taking the sequence OUT is what let the whole sentence be computed at once — the paper's real gift was not attention, it was parallelism.

request: Why did Malthus think population growth must end in famine, and was he right?
title: Malthus's two lines

elements.of: An Essay on the Principle of Population

commands.speak: Malthus, writing in 1798, put two quantities on one pair of axes.
Food, he argued, can only grow by addition — clear another field, drain another marsh. A straight line.
People grow by multiplication: every couple that has four children doubles the next generation. A curve that bends upward.
A line and a curve like that must meet, and after they meet there is not enough. Famine, he concluded, is not a policy failure but arithmetic.
The argument is his Essay on the Principle of Population — the book that got economics called the dismal science.
He was wrong for two centuries, and the mistake is in the straight line: fertiliser, new varieties and machinery made food grow by multiplication too.
The arithmetic was never the weak part. The assumption about which curve food follows was.

commands.speak: Here is a curve — anything whose value changes as x moves.
Now pick a single point on it and ask how fast the curve is rising THERE. The question sounds broken: a rate of change needs two points, and we have one.
The trick is to draw the one straight line that grazes the curve at that point without cutting through it.
The derivative is simply that line's slope — four tenths here: nudge x forward by one, and the line climbs by 0.4.
Which is why a derivative is a number, not a shape: the whole curve at that point has been replaced by one straight line, and all we kept is how steep it was.

Nothing distinguishes these urns. No urn is better. Only the rule is at work.
By a hundred and eighty-five balls, Urn E has taken the lead on thirty percent — and Urn B has fallen to seven and a half.
Four hundred and twenty-five balls, and the fan has stopped opening. Urn E is on thirty-two, Urn B on six and a half.
Eight hundred and twenty-five balls. Urn E has a third of them, Urn B a sixteenth — and the lead has not changed hands since the hundred and eighty-fifth ball.

request: Show how a correlation matrix settles down as the sample grows: n = 20, 50, 200, 1000

elements.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
def corr(n):
    a = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    b = 0.8 * a + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n)
    c = 0.5 * b + rng.normal(0, 0.9, n)
    noise = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    return np.corrcoef([a, b, c, noise]).round(2).tolist()
frames = [corr(n) for n in (20, 50, 200, 1000)]

commands.speak: Four measurements, built by a seeded script so we know the truth exactly: A with B is zero point eight, B with C is zero point four nine, A with C is zero point three nine — and the fourth variable is pure noise, correlated with nothing.
This is what twenty draws say. B against C reads zero point seven seven, more than half again the truth, and the noise column is already warm.
Every cell here is an estimate, and at n of twenty the estimates are bad.
Fifty draws. B against C falls to zero point five four, but the noise column is still finding a correlation of zero point two where there is none.
Two hundred draws: zero point four four, and the noise has cooled to almost nothing.
A thousand, and the matrix has settled onto the truth — zero point seven nine, zero point five, zero point three nine, and a noise column that has faded out.
The same structure produced all four of these pictures. A correlation is not something you read off a matrix. It is an estimate, and n is what you pay for it.

request: Show how Norwegian health spending splits between curative care, long-term care and medicines, and how that split changed from 2005 to 2023

commands.speak: Norwegian health spending, from Statistics Norway's health accounts — table ten eight one four — at four points between 2005 and 2023, in current kroner, rounded to the nearest hundred million.
In 2005 the country spent about a hundred and sixty-six billion kroner on health, and curative care took roughly forty-nine percent of it.
By 2011 the total was about two hundred and forty-five billion. By 2017, about three hundred and forty.
And in 2023, about four hundred and seventy-four billion — very nearly three times the 2005 figure in current kroner.

Now look at the shape rather than the height. Curative care was about forty-nine percent of the total in 2005, and about forty-nine percent in 2023. Long-term care went from roughly twenty-six percent to twenty-seven.

Only one of the four fell as a share: medicines and other goods dispensed outside hospital, from about fourteen percent to about eleven. This is not a country changing its priorities. It is the same shape, three times bigger.

commands.speak: microdata.no holds the income of every person in Norway — and you never get to see a single one of them. So how do you ask it anything?
You write a script. This first line says which register database we are asking: the FDB, version fifty-four, which we will call fd.

request: Show a Commodore 64 switched on, tell what made it the best-selling computer ever, and let me play a game on it

commands.speak: A beige box with a keyboard, plugged into the family television — and this blue screen, waiting.
Nineteen eighty-two, five hundred and ninety-five dollars. Then Commodore cut the price, and cut it again, until it was the computer a family could actually buy.
Seventeen million of them — still the best-selling single model of computer there has ever been. That number is why so many programmers of a certain age learned on this screen.
The blue screen is not decoration. It is BASIC: type a line, press RETURN, the machine obeys. Every C64 booted straight into a programming language, which is a thing computers stopped doing.
And it had a sound chip, the SID, that musicians still write for. Games were what most people used it for — so here is one.
Find your way out of the maze. Close the emulator when you have had enough, and we go on.
Every one of those seventeen million came with the same blue screen and the same READY. That is where a great many careers began.

request: Type your first Commodore 64 BASIC program on the machine: clear the screen, print a line five times, turn the border black — then let me play a lander written in ten lines

elements.code:
10 PRINT CHR$(147)
20 FOR I=1 TO 5
30 PRINT "HELLO, WORLD"
40 NEXT I
50 POKE 53280,0
60 POKE 53281,0

commands.speak: A Commodore 64 boots into BASIC. Every line starts with a number, and the machine keeps them in order. This one clears the screen — CHR$ one-forty-seven is the character that does it.
That number is the whole secret: on this machine, clearing the screen is printing a character.
A loop. FOR I equals one TO five, print, NEXT. Three lines, and the machine repeats the middle one five times.
And two POKEs. Fifty-three thousand two hundred and eighty is the border, eighty-one the background. Zero is black.
A POKE writes one byte straight into a chip's register. No API, no permission — the address IS the interface.
RUN. Five greetings on a black screen. That is the entire program, and it is drawn here exactly as the machine would show it.
Now, a lander in ten lines of BASIC someone else wrote. Same machine, same language — but this one you can fly.
Land softly. Close the emulator when you are done, and we go on.

commands.speak: A Commodore 64, switched on. It is not waiting for a program. It is waiting for you: type a line, press RETURN, and it answers on the next.
PRINT two plus two.
Four — with a space in front of it, where a minus sign would go, and READY. under it. The machine is done, and it says so every time.
POKE writes one byte straight into the video chip. Fifty-three thousand two hundred and eighty is the border.
Black. No menu, no setting, one number.
And eighty-one is the background.
Colours are characters too: printing character one-fifty-eight switches the ink to yellow before the word.
That is the whole interface. Every line you type is a conversation with a chip, and it always ends with READY.
